title: The Namami Gange Ganga Cleaning Mission Shortfall
dek: India's flagship river-cleaning programme promised a clean Ganga by 2020, backed by thousands of crores in funding. A decade on, government audits themselves have found sewage treatment plants that don't work, untreated waste still pouring in, and funds left unused.

heroStat.label: of sewage still flowing largely untreated into the Ganga's main stem in Uttar Pradesh according to CAG audit findings

promise.quote: Namami Gange will achieve effective abatement of pollution and rejuvenation of the river Ganga, with a clean and continuously flowing Ganga.
promise.madeBy: Government of India, National Mission for Clean Ganga
promise.role: Central government mission under the Ministry of Jal Shakti responsible for the Ganga rejuvenation programme
promise.context: Launched in 2014-15 with an initial outlay of around Rs 20,000 crore, later expanded, Namami Gange funded sewage treatment plants, drain interception, and river-front works across states along the Ganga, with informal targets to visibly clean the river by 2019-2020.

target.description: Sewage treatment infrastructure built and functioning to treat the bulk of wastewater generated by towns along the Ganga before it reaches the river, meeting National Green Tribunal pollution norms, within the mission's funded timelines.
target.standard: National Green Tribunal water-quality norms for the Ganga and the mission's own stated objectives and funding timelines.

reality.description: More than a decade after launch and with well over Rs 30,000 crore sanctioned nationally, government audits have repeatedly found the programme falling short of its own targets. A CAG audit of Namami Gange works in Uttarakhand (2025) found sewage treatment plants with defective designs, poor maintenance, drains that were never actually tapped and connected to treatment plants, and waste dumped near the river despite funds being available. A separate CAG review found over a third of sewage treatment plants examined were sending untreated or partially treated sewage into the river, and of 44 plants inspected only three to five met National Green Tribunal compliance norms. Officials estimate towns along the Ganga's main stem generate around 3,600 million litres of sewage per day, of which only about 2,100 MLD is being treated, leaving over 1,500 MLD flowing into the river largely untreated.

gap.metricLabel: Sewage generated by towns on the Ganga's main stem vs. sewage actually being treated
gap.note: Figures are as reported in CAG and related audit coverage and vary somewhat by year and source; they illustrate the scale of the persistent treatment gap rather than a single precisely reconciled national figure.

money.allocatedLabel: Initial Namami Gange outlay approved in 2014-15 (subsequently expanded in later phases)
money.releasedLabel: Total funds released to states and implementing agencies
money.spentLabel: Total funds utilised on completed, functioning infrastructure
money.notes: CAG audits in individual states, including Uttarakhand, have separately flagged unutilised or underutilised funds even where sewage treatment infrastructure remained incomplete or non-functional; this investigation did not find a single reconciled national utilisation figure.

timeline.label: Namami Gange launched
timeline.detail: The central government approved the integrated Ganga rejuvenation mission with an initial outlay of around Rs 20,000 crore.

timeline.label: Original clean-Ganga timeline lapses
timeline.detail: Informal government commitments to show a visibly cleaner Ganga by around 2019-2020 were not met; independent reporting found continued pollution levels.

timeline.label: CAG inspection finds most plants non-compliant
timeline.detail: Of 44 sewage treatment plants inspected, only three to five were found compliant with National Green Tribunal norms.

timeline.label: CAG report on Uttarakhand finds implementation failures
timeline.detail: A CAG performance audit found defectively designed plants, unconnected drains, and continued dumping of waste near the river despite funding availability.

legalStatus.summary: This is a programme-implementation failure documented through the Comptroller and Auditor General's constitutional audit function, not a criminal case. No individual has been prosecuted; accountability has been limited to audit findings and parliamentary scrutiny.

verdict.summary: That Namami Gange has fallen well short of its clean-Ganga promise is not seriously disputed — it is documented by the government's own auditor, the CAG, across multiple state-level reports spanning a decade. What remains unresolved is a fix: successive audits keep finding the same categories of failure (non-functional plants, unconnected drains, unspent funds) years apart.
verdict.reasoning: The core finding — that treatment capacity has consistently lagged sewage generation and that CAG audits have repeatedly found implementation failures — is corroborated by the government's own constitutional auditor across multiple independent reports, not merely by advocacy or opposition claims.

incomplete: This investigation did not identify one single reconciled national figure for total Namami Gange funds sanctioned, released and spent to date, since figures vary by phase and by state-level audit.
Current (post-2025) river water-quality data was not independently reviewed here; the entry relies on the most recent CAG and independent reporting available.
Whether any individual officials or contractors faced disciplinary or criminal action over specific defective works (e.g. in Uttarakhand) was not established in sources reviewed.
